--- title: "Version it, pin it, publish it" subtitle: "Reproducible Workflows · Session 3" format: revealjs: footer: A. Stamm · Reproducible Workflows · Session 3 --- # Recap: Sessions 1 & 2 → Session 3 ## Where we are {.inv} You have a working, versioned **portfolio book**; today we make it durable and shareable. ::: {.incremental} - Session 1: **write**, Quarto documents, transparency. - Session 2: **source**, real data, cleaned, pinned, and under git in your book's Chapter 1. - Session 3 (today): **deepen git** (PRs, review), **pin the environment** (uvr), **fix randomness** (`{withr}`), **publish** (Posit Connect), and **finish Chapter 1**. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} Trade "it works on my machine" for: versioned, pinned (version + packages), published at a URL anyone can open. ::: # Deepen your git ## Why version control (recap) {.inv} Your smallest reproducible unit is not a file: it's the *history of changes* to a project. ::: {.incremental} - **Undo anything**: every state of your project is recoverable. - **Answer "what changed and when?"**: a full log of your analysis's evolution. - **Collaborate safely**: branches, PRs, review, no clobbering. - **A backup that lives off-machine**: your laptop dying stops being a catastrophe. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} Git is the time-machine around your analysis; today we make the habit rigorous enough to share and review. ::: ## Commit, branch, push: already yours {.inv} You built these reflexes in Session 2; today we sharpen them: ::: {.term}
$
git status # your compass: where am I?
$
git add # stage what you want to keep
$
git commit -m "message" # snapshot with a note
$
git checkout -b # never work on main ::: ::: {.incremental} - **Commit often**: small, descriptive commits beat rare mega-commits. - **Never push to `main`**: a PR is how a change reaches the shared history. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} `usethis::use_git()` and the Positron source-control pane do all of this with clicks. ::: ## Keep a branch aligned with main {.inv} Before you touch a branch, fold in whatever `main` gained, so you never diverge silently: ::: {.term}
$
git checkout main
$
git fetch --all --prune # see remote changes
$
git pull # bring main up to date
$
git checkout
$
git merge main # fold main into your branch ::: ::: {.callout-desc} Do this **before** changing a branch, and your branch tracks `main`: conflicts largely disappear. ::: ## A conflict, and what it looks like {.inv} Two people change the same line, git can't choose: it marks the file for you. ::: {.split-2} ::: {.term} # my-analysis.R (merge conflict) ::: {.cell} ::: ::: ::: {.term} # a genuine .csv conflict also shows this ::: {.cell} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - Text between `<<<<<<<` and `>>>>>>>` is what each side proposed; delete the markers and keep the right answer. - In Positron: use the **inline merge editor** (Source Control → merge) to pick upstream / incoming / both. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} A conflict just means two edits touched the same place: resolve deliberately, commit, move on. ::: ## Pull requests {.inv} A PR is "please merge my branch into `main`", reviewed before it lands: ::: {.incremental} - **Positron way**: the **Source Control** pane → create a pull request via the GitHub extension from your pushed branch. - **GitHub way**: push the branch, then GitHub's web UI offers "Compare & pull request" from the repo page. - A PR is the *reviewable unit*: it's where your Chapter 1 gets feedback. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} Merge to `main` **only via a PR**; `main` stays an always-working, always-reproducible line. ::: ## Review, comment, accept {.inv} A PR is a conversation, not just a merge button: ::: {.incremental} - **Assign a reviewer** (your instructor, a classmate) to the PR. - **Comment on specific lines**: both sides of the diff can leave notes. - **Request changes** or **approve**: the author updates the branch, pushes, and the PR updates. - Works the same in Positron (GitHub extension) and on the GitHub web site. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} Review is how your work becomes reproducible to another human; you'll use this on Chapter 1. ::: ## Your instructor, in the loop {.paper} ::: {.paper-card} Reserve a branch per idea (e.g. `eda-chapter-1`), push it, and open a **draft PR** when you'd like feedback: - During the gap and today, the PR is how your instructor comments on and reviews your Chapter 1. - Address comments, push, and the PR updates; no emailing files around. :::
Going further

happygitwithr (happygitwithr.com) is the tutorial this course follows. Its pull-requests chapter walks the whole review loop step by step, with screenshots, for both the Positron and terminal routes.

# Pin your environment: `uvr` (and `renv`) ## The moving-environment problem {.inv} Your analysis depended on package *versions*, which silently change: ::: {.incremental} - `install.packages()` updates packages **globally**, and today's tidyverse may differ from last month's. - The **R version itself** also moves: a book may render today and break next year on a newer R. - "Works on my machine" becomes "worked on *that* machine, that day". ::: ::: {.callout-desc} The fix: **pin** the versions your project needs, committed with the code. `renv` pins packages; `uvr` also pins the **R version**. ::: ## renv: the state of the art {.inv} `renv` gives each project its own library and a lockfile of versions: ::: {.term}
$
renv::init() # project-private library + renv.lock
$
renv::snapshot() # record current versions
$
renv::restore() # rebuild the library FROM the lockfile ::: ::: {.incremental} - **Commit `renv.lock`**: a machine-readable list of every version. - **`.gitignore` `renv/library/`**: the cache stays out of git. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} `renv` is the solid, established tool: it pins packages. `uvr` also pins the R version, so that's our focus. ::: ## uvr: pin R itself, not just packages {.inv} `uvr` wraps `uv` (the Python manager) so R gets the same "one engine, both languages" discipline: ::: {.incremental} - **`uvr::init()`** sets up a project manifest + lockfile (a `uv` project). - **`uvr::r_install("4.6.1")`** installs a project-managed R version. - **`uvr::r_pin("4.6.1")`** records that version in the manifest, so it's **committed and reproducible**. - **`uvr::add("tidyverse")`** adds to the manifest, regenerates the lockfile, and installs, all in one call. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} `r_list()` shows versions; `r_use()` picks one for the session, `r_pin()` records it in the project (that's what survives a fresh clone). ::: ## Install uvr {.inv} The companion R package from GitHub, then the `uvr` binary: ::: {.term}
>
pak::pak("nbafrank/uvr-r") # the uvr R package, from GitHub
>
uvr::install_uvr() # installs the uvr binary (cross-platform) ::: ::: {.incremental} - One-time setup: the R package is the interface; `install_uvr()` puts the engine on your machine. - It relies on `uv`, the same tool that manages Python later in your book. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} Installing the R package first, then the binary, keeps the whole `uvr` workflow runnable from R functions inside your project. ::: ## What a lockfile actually pins {.inv} Both lockfiles are plain text, and that's the point. Open one and it reads like a shopping list: ::: {.callout-desc} `uv.lock` (via uvr) records each R/Python package with **exact version + hashes**; `renv.lock` records each R package + version + source. Neither stores the packages, only the recipe to rebuild them; `uvr` adds the **pinned R version** on top. ::: ::: {.split-2} ::: {.term} # uvr / uv.lock (excerpt) [[package]] name = "dplyr" version = "1.1.4" hash = "sha256:2f3a9..." # and R itself is pinned too requires-python = ">=4.6.1" ::: ::: {.term} # renv.lock (excerpt) "dplyr": { "Version": "1.1.4", "Source": "CRAN" } ::: ::: ::: {.callout-desc} A lockfile isn't magic; it's an explicit, machine-readable record of what you ran with. Diff it over time to see exactly when an environment changed. ::: ## R and Python, side by side {.inv} Every reproducibility tool you've met has an equivalent in Python, with the same ideas: | Role | R | Python | |---|---|---| | **Environment** | [`uvr`](https://nbafrank.github.io/uvr/) / [`renv`](https://rstudio.github.io/renv/) | [`uv`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) | | **Data & artifacts** | [`{pins}`](https://pins.rstudio.com) | [`pins`](https://rstudio.github.io/pins-python/) | | **Model versioning/deploy** | [`{vetiver}`](https://rstudio.github.io/vetiver-r/) | [`vetiver`](https://rstudio.github.io/vetiver-python/) | ::: {.callout-desc} `uvr` literally runs on `uv`, so R and Python share one engine. Your book is Python-compatible by design, and the reproducible pipeline is the same in both languages. ::: # Reproducible habits: randomness ## Random numbers break reproducibility {.inv} Any code that uses randomness gives a different answer on every run, unless told otherwise: ::: {.incremental} - Sampling, simulations, plot jitter, cross-validation splits: all change a figure or number each render. - A bare `set.seed()` at the top of a document leaks into the whole session and never restores it. - Result: the same `.qmd` renders "differently", so a reader can't reproduce your exact figure. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} A document whose figure changes every render isn't reproducible. Fix the seed **where the randomness happens**, not globally. ::: ## Scope a seed with `{withr}` {.inv} `{withr}` sets an option for one block and restores it afterward, locally and explicitly: ::: {.codewindow .r width="100%" name="reproducible-figure.qmd"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] Gentoo Adelie Chinstrap Adelie Adelie Levels: Adelie Chinstrap Gentoo ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - `withr::with_seed(seed, { ... })`: set the seed for exactly that expression. - `withr::local_seed(seed)` inside a chunk: same idea, restored when the chunk ends. - Fix the figure *inside the cell that draws it*; every render then matches. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} Make randomness intentional and local; your Chapter 1's figures become exactly reproducible without leaking a seed into the session. ::: # Publish it ## What Posit Connect is {.inv} A published analysis is one anyone can *open at a URL*, with no local environment required: ::: {.incremental} - **Posit Connect** hosts R and Python content (books, reports, apps, dashboards) behind a stable URL. - Publishing pushes your **rendered** book to the server; readers just open the link. - This is the "anywhere" end of the spectrum: reachable, shareable, current. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} A URL is the end state of the loop: data → analysis → report → versioned → **published**. ::: ## Pushing a Quarto book {.inv} Rendering is local and reproducible; *publishing* is a one-step deploy: ::: {.term}
$
quarto render # build the book (local, reproducible)
$
quarto publish connect # push to Posit Connect ::: ::: {.incremental} - First publish asks you to log in / configure the server once. - Every later publish updates the same URL: your portfolio stays current. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} The URL shares work *outside* the notebook: an employer, a teammate, or your future self all see the same, current, reproducible book. ::: ## Proof: reproduce it on a blank machine {.inv} The real test of everything this course taught: hand someone the *recipe* and see if the book reappears: ::: {.term}
$
git clone # 1. get the source + history
$
uvr::restore() (or renv::restore) # 2. rebuild env + R version
$
quarto render # 3. rebuild the book ::: ::: {.incremental} - **Three commands, no "works on my machine"**: a second person (or your future self) rebuilds your exact book. - If this *doesn't* work on a fresh clone, you've found a reproducibility gap to fix. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} Publishing gives a URL to *send*; `clone + restore + render` proves the loop closed. ::: ## The full loop, closed {.inv} Everything this course taught, in one connected picture: ::: {.incremental} 1. **Write** the analysis in Quarto: source *is* the report. 2. **Source** the data by code: `{pins}` versions the fetched copy. 3. **Version** with git: every step reversible, reviewed via PRs. 4. **Pin** your environment with `uvr`/`uv`. 5. **Deploy** your model with `{vetiver}`, pinned like your data. 6. **Publish** to a URL: reachable and shareable. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} Miss any link and the chain weakens. Keep all six and your analysis is reproducible by anyone, anywhere, at any time. ::: # Portfolio handoff ## How your book keeps growing {.inv} Your Chapter 1 was the seed: now it's part of a living artefact: ::: {.incremental} - Later courses **append chapters** to your book (`02-semester-2.qmd`, `03-semester-3.qmd`): the placeholders you kept are the roadmap. - Because everything is versioned, pinned, and published, those additions are themselves reproducible. - By term's end: a multi-chapter, multi-language, published portfolio. ::: ::: {.callout-desc} The conventions you followed make it easy for other instructors to build *on your work*. ::: ## Your EDA chapter: the rubric {.paper} ::: {.paper-card} **How Chapter 1 will be assessed**: use this as your checklist for the work block that follows: | Criterion | Looks like | |---|---| | **Question** | a clear one-sentence motivation up front | | **Reproducible data** | fetched by code and pinned with `{pins}`; provenance recorded | | **Cleaning decisions** | documented *why*, not just *what* | | **Evidence** | captioned figures, each referred to in prose | | **Honesty** | states what was found *and* what wasn't | | **Structure** | the 5-section recipe (≈ IMRAD) | :::
Going further

A chapter that nails these is a chapter that will stand up in a job interview, not just a graded assignment. The rubric maps onto IMRAD: question ≈ introduction, data + cleaning ≈ methods, figures ≈ results, and your closing reflection ≈ discussion.

## Your turn: finish Chapter 1 (most of the session) {.paper} ::: {.paper-card} **Work block (the rest of the session).** Turn the EDA you built into a *finished* Chapter 1, then publish it. 1. Apply the rubric: complete the question, cleaning decisions, captions, and findings. 2. **Pin** your data (`{pins}`) and environment (`uvr`); scope randomness with `{withr}`. 3. **Commit to a branch**, push, open a PR, address the instructor's review. 4. **Publish** the book to Posit Connect and open the URL. :::
Going further

This is the moment everything this course taught comes together: source by code, clean with evidence, pin data and environment, version by git, review by PR, publish to a URL. Ask the instructor and your neighbours for review as you go; that peer review is part of the grade and part of the habit.

## Models and the Python side {.inv} Your portfolio may grow models and extra languages: same reproducible pipeline, meeting them at the door: ::: {.incremental} - **[`{vetiver}`](https://rstudio.github.io/vetiver-r/)** pins a trained **model** + the versions that built it, right beside your data on the same board. - Where a later chapter ships a model, `{vetiver}` gives it a version to deploy, not just `saveRDS()` and hope. - **Python twins** for everything: [`uvr`](https://nbafrank.github.io/uvr/) / [`renv`](https://rstudio.github.io/renv/)↔[`uv`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), [`{pins}`](https://pins.rstudio.com)↔[`pins`](https://rstudio.github.io/pins-python/), [`{vetiver}`](https://rstudio.github.io/vetiver-r/)↔[`vetiver`](https://rstudio.github.io/vetiver-python/). ::: ::: {.callout-desc} The rubric's criteria scale to any language: source by code, pin data *and* models, version, publish. A `{vetiver}` model re-deploys anywhere. ::: ## Gallery walk / peer review {.paper} ::: {.paper-card} **Wrap (≈15 min).** Open **two classmates'** published books and give feedback on: - the **first figure**: can you read its caption and the story it tells? - the **cleaning section**: could you justify the same decisions in your own words? - the **findings**: are they specific and honest? - the **URL**: does it open and work as a finished publication? Use the rubric: 2 things they did well, 1 thing to improve. :::
Going further

Post your book's URL in the shared space; comment on two classmates' via their PRs or a short note. Peer review is the last reproducibility habit: your work is only reproducible if another human can navigate it, and a URL is what makes that test real.

## Three moves, one career {.dark auto-animate=true background-color="#17251F"} ::: {.big-title data-id="title" style="left:88px; top:150px; width:720px; font-size:72px;"} Write, version, publish. ::: ::: {.panel data-id="draft" style="left:840px; top:150px; width:150px; height:360px;"} ::: ::: {.panel data-id="review" style="left:1006px; top:150px; width:150px; height:170px;"} ::: ::: {.panel data-id="release" style="left:1006px; top:340px; width:150px; height:170px;"} ::: ## You built this {.light auto-animate=true background-color="#F1EEE6"} ::: {.big-title data-id="title" style="left:92px; top:104px; width:1100px; font-size:44px;"} By the end of this course you can turn any analysis into a versioned, pinned, published, reproducible portfolio. ::: ::: {.panel .card data-id="draft" style="left:96px; top:220px; width:340px; height:360px;"} [Write]{.h} [Your analysis lives in a Quarto doc: source *is* the report.]{.p} ::: ::: {.panel .card data-id="review" style="left:470px; top:220px; width:340px; height:360px;"} [Source & Version]{.h} [Data and models **pinned** (`{pins}`/`{vetiver}`); history kept by git (branches, PRs); environment and R version pinned by uvr.]{.p} ::: ::: {.panel .card data-id="release" style="left:844px; top:220px; width:340px; height:360px;"} [Publish]{.h} [The whole thing behind a URL anyone can open, reproducible anywhere.]{.p} ::: ## Your portfolio, published {.light auto-animate=true background-color="#F1EEE6"} ::: {.big-title data-id="title" style="left:92px; top:104px; width:1100px; font-size:44px;"} From one-off report to a career you keep. ::: ::: {.panel .card data-id="release" style="left:96px; top:200px; width:800px; height:400px;"} [Every chapter is a reproducible chapter]{.h} [Everything from this course (the Quarto report you `source()` from, the git history, the `uvr`/`uv` lockfile, the published URL) stacks into one portfolio you keep growing. That is the reproducible habit, made visible.]{.p style="font-size:24px; line-height:1.6;"} ::: ::: {.panel .marker data-id="draft" style="left:944px; top:230px;"} ::: ::: {.panel .marker data-id="review" style="left:944px; top:290px;"} ::: ## Thank you: keep the habit {.dark .finale auto-animate=true background-color="#17251F"} ::: {.big-title data-id="title" style="left:140px; top:300px; width:1000px; font-size:54px; text-align:center;"} Reproducible is a habit, not a tool. ::: ::: {.panel data-id="draft" style="left:470px; top:150px; width:110px; height:110px;"} ::: ::: {.panel data-id="review" style="left:590px; top:150px; width:110px; height:110px;"} ::: ::: {.panel data-id="release" style="left:710px; top:150px; width:110px; height:110px;"} ::: ::: {style="position:absolute; left:96px; top:600px; width:1024px; font-size:17px; color:rgba(241,238,230,0.62);"} Keep your portfolio growing: every course adds a chapter, and every chapter is reproducible by default. <script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
